qabala: Gabala was the ancient capital of Caucasian Albania, and archaeological evidence indicates that it served as capital as early as the 4th century BCE. Excavations near the village of Chukhur show that from the 4th or 3rd century BCE until the 18th century it was one of the main cities of the region, with developed trade and crafts. It stood on the Silk Road. Pliny called it Cabalaca, the geographer Ptolemy Khabala, the Armenian geographer Anania Shirakatsi Kavalak, and the 9th-century historian al-Baladhuri al-Khazar. Until the Shirvanshahs occupied it, a local Caucasian Albanian family ruled it, the last known member of which was Abd al-Barr ibn Anbasa.

Gabala was taken in turn by the Shirvanshah Fariburz and King David IV of Georgia in 1120, by Timur in 1386, by the Safavid shah Tahmasib I in 1538 and by Nader Shah in 1734, yet preserved its culture and identity. After Nader Shah died in 1747 the region broke into independent khanates and sultanates, and Gabala became the Qutqashen Sultanate, later absorbed into the Sheki Khanate. After the Russian annexation of the region the khanates were ended in 1841 and the territory was incorporated into Russian governorates, Gabala falling within the Elisabethpol Governorate.

Qabala is the administrative centre of the Qabala District of Azerbaijan. Its municipality consists of the town and the village of Küsnat. Until Azerbaijan's independence the town was called Kutkashen; it was then renamed in honour of the much older city of Gabala. Because of the archaeological finds, the ancient site was declared a National State Reserve in 1985. Its ruins include a walled city and the main gate of Caucasian Albania.

Since 2009 the town has hosted the Gabala International Music Festival, which includes classical and jazz performers. Many rivers rise in the district, as its mountainous relief and humid climate produce a dense river network belonging to the left-bank tributaries of the Kura basin.
qaboos-bin-said: Qaboos was born in Salalah, in Dhofar, on 18 November 1940, the only son of Sultan Said bin Taimur and Sheikha Mazoon bint Ahmad Al Mashani. He was educated at a private institution in Pune, India, and from the age of 16 at a private school in Bury St Edmunds, England. He entered the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst at 20, graduated in September 1962, and served with the 1st Battalion, The Cameronians (Scottish Rifles), in Germany for a year. When he returned to Oman in late 1966 his father placed him under virtual house arrest in Al Hosn Palace in Salalah, where he studied Islam, Islamic law and the history of Oman.

Qaboos took the throne on 23 July 1970 in a coup against his father, supported by the British. He declared that Muscat and Oman would be known as the Sultanate of Oman, to reflect its political unity. His first problem was the Dhofar Rebellion (1962–1976), an armed communist insurgency from South Yemen. The sultanate defeated it with help from the Shah of Iran, Jordanian troops, British Special Forces and the Royal Air Force.

Oman then had only 10 km of paved roads. Qaboos used oil revenue to build schools, hospitals, roads, a telecommunications network, ports and universities, and he achieved electrification. He abolished slavery in his first year. The state was an absolute monarchy: he was also prime minister, minister of foreign affairs and minister of defence, and all legislation, including the Basic Law of 1996, was issued by royal decree. Oman stayed neutral between Iran and its Arab neighbours and often acted as an intermediary. His reign is known as the Omani Renaissance.

Qaboos was an Ibadi Muslim who granted freedom of religion and financed Catholic and Protestant churches and Hindu temples as well as mosques, among them the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque. He married his cousin Sayyida Nawwal in 1976; the marriage ended in divorce in 1979 and he had no children.

He had colon cancer from 2014 and died on 10 January 2020, aged 79. He named no heir publicly. Under the constitution the Royal Family Council had three days to choose a sultan, and if it failed, a letter in his hand would be opened. The council deferred to that letter on 11 January, which named his cousin Haitham bin Tariq as sultan.
qadi: The term qadi was in use from the time of Muhammad and remained the word for a judge throughout Islamic history. The office as a delegated post arose under the first Umayyad caliphs, between 661 and 705 CE, when provincial governors of the new empire could not settle the many disputes among Muslims and began to hand the task to others. No body of Islamic law yet existed, so the first qadis decided cases from Arab customary law, the laws of the conquered territories, the precepts of the Qur'an and their own sense of equity.

In the later Umayyad period a class of legal scholars, distinct from the qadis, supplied the missing body of law, and by the Abbasid accession in 750 their work was essentially complete. They took the qadis' precedents as their starting point. Once the law was formed, a qadi was expected to adhere to it alone.

A qadi remained the delegate of a higher authority, ultimately the caliph or the ruler of a territory, so judicial and executive power were not separated. The Abbasid caliphs created the office of chief qadi, and Abu Yusuf, a disciple of Abu Hanifa, was among the earliest. The Mamluk Sultanate, which ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250 to 1516, appointed four chief qadis, one for each Sunni school of law.

A qadi had to be free, sane, an adult, trustworthy and a Muslim. His court was a one-judge court, held in a public place, often the chief mosque, and his judgements could not be appealed. Beyond the courtroom he administered religious endowments, executed wills and guarded orphans. In practice the mazalim court, presided over by the ruler or his governor, heard complaints against unfair decisions, and the shurtah took over criminal justice, leaving the qadi chiefly inheritance, personal status, property and commerce.

Qadis served in the Songhai Empire, where they sat in trading towns such as Timbuktu and Djenné, in Al-Andalus, and in the Ottoman Empire, where they also coordinated city services. In the Indian subcontinent the post often passed from father to son, and qazi families kept lands and standing in their towns. The Spanish word alcalde, now a mayor, derives from the Arabic al-qaḍi; Castile, Leon and Portugal adopted it in the eleventh and twelfth centuries for assistant judges.
qajar-dynasty: The Qajars were heads of the Turkoman Qajar tribe within the Qizilbash confederacy, the Turkoman warriors who formed the main force of the Safavid army. A contingent of Qajars was among the 7,000 tribal soldiers with whom Ismail marched from Erzincan to Shirvan, and although the tribe was smaller than others it played a major part in important events of the 16th century. The dynasty gained prominence with the rise of Shahverdi Sultan in the early 16th century.

The immediate ancestor of the Qajar monarchs, Shah Qoli Khan of the Quvanlu of Ganja, married into the Quvanlu Qajars of Astarabad. His son Fath-Ali Khan, a noted military commander under the Safavid shahs, was killed in 1726. Fath-Ali Khan's son Mohammad Hasan Khan (1722-1758) was the father of Agha Mohammad Khan, and he was killed on the orders of Karim Khan of the Zand dynasty.

The Qajars used their tribal alliances and military strength to unify the country amid the post-Safavid chaos. The Unification of Iran, from 1779 to 1796, was the work of Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, who reigned from 1789 to 1797, and the dynasty ruled Iran until 1925. Its effective rule ended when the Majlis, meeting as a constituent assembly on 12 December 1925, declared Reza Shah, a former brigadier-general of the Persian Cossack Brigade, the new shah, which began the reign of the Pahlavi dynasty. A Russian branch of the family belonged to the Russian nobility, and its members held senior posts in the Imperial Russian Army.

The shahs took grand titles, among them Shahanshah of Iran, Zell'ollah (Shadow of God on earth) and Qebleh-ye 'ālam (Pivot of the Universe). These served to legitimise their rule amid internal and external challenges, and blended pre-Islamic, Islamic-Shi'i and nomadic elements of Persian governance. The dynasty built many royal residences, of which the Golestan and Niavaran Palace Complexes in Tehran are the most prominent. Among Qajar women, Princess Tadj al-Saltaneh, a daughter of Naser-din-Shah, co-founded the first Iranian women's rights movement, Anjoman Naswan, and wrote the first memoir by an Iranian woman.
qalat-al-bahrain: Qal'at al-Bahrain stands on the northern shore of Bahrain Island, about 6 kilometres from Manama on the fertile north coast. It is a tell, an artificial mound about 12 metres high built up by successive layers of human occupation, the largest tell in the Persian Gulf region. It was built close to the port and partly on land reclaimed from the shore. The site covers 17.5 hectares and has been called Bahrain's most important site in antiquity. The name means fort of Bahrain, and the fort on top of the mound, Qalʿat al-Burtughal, the Portuguese fort, gave the whole site its name.

The layers show a continuous human presence from about 2300 BCE. The earliest settlement on the northern side was a small village, the only one of its period in eastern Arabia, whose people grew crops near the oasis, planted palms, kept cattle, sheep and goats and fished. Their houses were of rough stone with clay or mortar and had plastered floors, and streets separated the housing blocks.

Later a walled town grew up, whose fortifications enclosed about 15 hectares and were raised several times, as the gates at four levels show. Streets 12 metres wide ran north to south, and a palace with warehouses stood at the centre. The place prospered until 1800 BCE, after which it was deserted and covered by drifting sand.

It was once the capital of the Dilmun civilisation. According to the Epic of Gilgamesh, Dilmun was the land of immortality, the ancestral place of the Sumerians and a meeting point of gods. Copper was cast in a large workshop and traded to Oman and Mesopotamia. Finds link the site with Mesopotamia through a cuneiform inscription and hematite, with Oman through steatite bowls, and with the Indus Civilization through carnelian beads and a stone weight. Later occupants included Kassites, Greeks, Portuguese and Persians.

A Danish expedition under Geoffrey Bibby excavated the site from 1954 to 1972, and a French expedition from the National Centre for Scientific Research worked there from the 1970s. About 50 cuneiform tablets were found, three of them dated to the reign of a Kassite king named Agum. Danish and Bahrain archaeologists have dug there since 1987, and about 25 percent of the site has been excavated. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
qanat: A qanat, or kariz, was developed in ancient Iran, originating approximately 3,000 years ago. According to most sources, Iranians created the technology in the early 1st millennium BCE and it spread slowly westward and eastward; other sources suggest a south-eastern Arabian origin, and similar systems appear to have been developed independently in China and in southern Peru. One theory holds that the qanat was devised to irrigate cotton fields in what is now Iran, doubling the water available for irrigation and urban use, which gave Persia larger agricultural surpluses and so more urbanisation and social stratification.

The word comes from Akkadian qanû, meaning reed. It is called foggara in Algeria and falaj in Oman. Qanat-style systems reached parts of Europe under the Roman Empire and were built on a larger scale in Muslim-ruled Spain. The Spanish introduced qanats into Mexico in 1520, and similar works at Nazca, called puquios, are dated by some archaeologists to about 500 CE.

A qanat is a gently sloping tunnel reached by a series of well-like vertical shafts. It taps groundwater, usually from an upland aquifer, and delivers it by gravity to a lower point without pumping. Because it runs underground, little water is lost to evaporation, and the system is fairly resistant to floods, earthquakes and wartime destruction.

Skilled labourers called muqannīs built qanats by hand, a well-paid profession usually passed from father to son. A crew of three or four began at the outlet and worked towards a test well dug where the mountains meet the alluvial fan, sinking shafts 20 to 35 metres apart. Fired clay hoops lined soft ground, and the shafts had to be cleaned and inspected regularly.

In Iranian towns, which often have several qanats, the water set the layout. The cleanest water was upstream, and more prosperous people lived at or just above the outlet. Water below the outlet ran in surface canals called jubs, and the streets followed them. Qanats supplied irrigation, drinking water and watermills, and air from them cooled an underground summer room, the shabestan. By 400 BCE Persian engineers could store ice through the summer in yakhchals.

Qanats still supply water in hot, arid regions. Among the largest working systems, besides those of Iran, are those of Afghanistan, Oman, Pakistan and the Turpan water system in Xinjiang. In Afghanistan more than 9,370 were in use in the twentieth century. Many long-inhabited settlements of West Asia and North Africa stand where conditions favoured a qanat.
qaqortoq: The area around Qaqortoq has been inhabited since prehistoric times, with a continuous human presence beginning with the Saqqaq culture roughly 4,300 years ago. Saqqaq sites are less prominent here than elsewhere in Greenland, with only sporadic finds such as chipped stone drills and carving knives. The Dorset people arrived about 2,800 years ago and left rectangular peat dwellings.

Written records of southern Greenland begin with the arrival of the Norse in the late 10th century. The ruins of Hvalsey, the most prominent Norse ruins in Greenland, lie 19 km north-east of the town. Trade between the Norse and the Thule people was at first scarce, but the southern Norse later traded with the southern Inuit and were for a time the main suppliers of ivory to northern Europe. The Norse era lasted almost five hundred years and ended in the mid-15th century; the last written record of it is of a wedding in the church at Hvalseyjarfjord in 1408. The Thule culture Inuit arrived around the 12th century and were contemporary with the Norse, though little evidence of early contact survives.

The present town was founded in 1775 by the Dano-Norwegian trader Anders Olsen on behalf of the General Trading Company. It was named Julianehaab after the Danish queen Juliane Marie. It became a major centre of the harp seal trade, and the Royal Greenland Trading Department long used it as a source of seal skins. The oldest standing building of the colonial harbour, a black-tarred log house of 1797, was designed by the royal Danish architect Kirkerup, pre-assembled in Denmark and reassembled on site. The museum occupies the former blacksmith's shop of 1804.

Qaqortoq, also called Julianehåb, is the capital of the Kujalleq municipality, formed on 1 January 2009 when the municipalities of Qaqortoq, Narsaq and Nanortalik merged. It has some 3,050 inhabitants and lies on the Qaqortoq Fjord beside the Labrador Sea. It is a seaport and the main centre of education in southern Greenland. Its Great Greenland Furhouse is the only tannery in Greenland. The town has an open-air sculpture project, Stone and Man, begun in 1993 to 1994, and the oldest fountain in Greenland, Mindebrønden, finished in 1932.
qara-khitai: The Qara Khitai, officially the Great Liao, was ruled by the Yelü clan of the Khitan people. The Khitans had ruled the Liao dynasty (907–1125) until the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty conquered it. In 1122 two groups of Khitans fled westward, one led by Yelü Dashi. In 1124 Dashi fled northwest and set up his headquarters at the garrison of Kedun on the Orkhon River, where 20,000 troops pledged allegiance and he took the title gurkhan, or universal khan. In 1130 he led his host further west.

Dashi conquered the Karakhanid city of Balasaghun in 1134, bringing the nearby Kankalis, Karluks, Kyrgyz and the Kingdom of Qocho under his overlordship, and in 1137 he defeated the Western Karakhanids near Khujand and annexed Fergana and Tashkent. On 9 September 1141 his army met the Seljuk forces of Ahmad Sanjar on the Qatwan steppe north of Samarkand. The Khitans encircled the Seljuks, and Sanjar barely escaped. Estimates of the dead range from 11,000 to 100,000, and the defeat cost the Seljuks all of Transoxiana. An attack on the Jin in 1134 failed, and Dashi gave up the hope of recovering northern China.

Dashi's widow Xiao Tabuyan ruled as regent from 1143 to 1150, followed by Yelü Yilie, Yelü Pusuwan and Yelü Zhilugu. Under Pusuwan the state held Balkh until 1198. In 1208 the Naiman prince Kuchlug, defeated by the Mongols, took refuge at the court and married Zhilugu's daughter, but in 1211 he revolted and captured Zhilugu while he was hunting. Genghis Khan sent his general Jebe in 1216, Kuchlug was captured and beheaded in 1218, and the Mongols fully conquered the former territories in 1220.

The Khitans ruled directly from Balasagun, in today's Kyrgyzstan, and the rest of the realm consisted of highly autonomous vassal states, among them Khwarazm, the Karluks, Qocho and the Karakhanids. The rulers kept much of the Liao administration, including Confucian forms, the Chinese calendar, reign names, Chinese-styled coins and imperial seals sent to vassals. A census under Yilie counted 84,500 households.

Chinese historians call the state the Western Liao and treat it as a legitimate Chinese dynasty. Muslim writers first called it Khitai and took up the name Qara Khitai after the Mongol invasions. The name Cathay derives from Khitai, and a Khitay tribe still lives in northern Kyrgyzstan.
qarmatians: The Qarmatians were an Isma'ili Shia militant movement led by an Arabized dynasty of Persian descent that claimed Alid descent. Under the Abbasid Caliphate various Shiite groups organised in secret opposition. After the death of Muhammad ibn Isma'il, most of the proto-Isma'ili Mubarakiyyah denied that he had died and recognised him as the Mahdi. Their missionary movement had great success in Khuzestan, where al-Husayn al-Ahwazi converted Hamdan in 874; he took the name Qarmat, and with his brother-in-law Abdan he prepared southern Iraq for the coming of the Mahdi. A change of leadership at Salamiyah in 899 split the movement, because the new leader, Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah, taught that Muhammad had died and that he himself was his descendant.

Their main stronghold was Bahrain, then covering much of eastern Arabia. The Zanj Rebellion in Basra had disrupted Abbasid power, and Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi, an Arabized Persian from Jannaba in Fars, took Hajr and al-Hasa in 899 and made al-Hasa his capital. The Qarmatians rejected the pilgrimage to Mecca as an illicit innovation and raided the pilgrim routes, and in 906 they massacred 20,000 pilgrims returning from Mecca. Under Abu Tahir al-Jannabi they came close to capturing Baghdad in 927 and sacked Mecca in 930, desecrating the Zamzam Well with the corpses of pilgrims and carrying off the Black Stone, which the Abbasids ransomed in 952.

For much of the tenth century they were the leading force in the Persian Gulf, collecting tribute from the caliph in Baghdad and from the Fatimids in Cairo, whose claim to the imamate they rejected. In 931 Abu Tahir handed power to a young Persian, Abu'l-Fadl al-Isfahani, whom the Qarmatians believed to be the Mahdi, but he executed nobles and insulted the prophets and was put to death after 80 days, which badly damaged the movement's credibility. After a defeat by the Abbasids in 976 the Qarmatians became a local power, and by the middle of the eleventh century the Uyunid dynasty had replaced them in Bahrain and eastern Arabia.

Their land had vast fruit and grain estates worked, according to Nasir Khusraw, who visited Hasa in 1051, by some thirty thousand Ethiopian slaves. He wrote that the people of Hasa paid no taxes and could borrow without interest. Some scholars have called the state proto-socialist, Perry Anderson called it an egalitarian slave-owning republic, and Azmi Bishara has called such claims an anachronistic projection of modern ideologies. In southern Iraq the Qarmatians were known as the Greengrocers because Abu Hatim al-Zutti forbade animal slaughter and certain vegetables.
qarshi: Qarshi was originally the Sogdian city of Nakhshab, which may have been called Eucratideia under the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom. It later became the Islamic Turkic city of Nasaf and then the Chagatay city of Qarshi, pronounced Kharsh; the modern name means fort. It lies in a fertile oasis producing wheat, cotton and silk, and was a stop on the 11-day caravan route between Balkh and Bukhara. The Chagataid khans Kebek and Qazan built palaces there, on the site of Chinggis Khaan's summer pasture, and in 1364 Timur built a fortified palace with moats.

The town developed steadily from the 14th century and grew rapidly under the Sheyban dynasty in the 16th. In the 18th century it was the second largest town of the Bukhara Khanate and, with the decline of Shahrisabz, the seat of the crown prince of the Emirate of Bukhara. It then had a double set of walls, ten caravanserais and four madrassahs. Russia annexed the Zarafshan Valley by 1868, and in 1873 the treaty making Bukhara a Russian protectorate was signed in Qarshi.

Qarshi is the capital of Qashqadaryo Region in southern Uzbekistan, about 520 km south-south-west of Tashkent, and is known for natural gas and for woven flat carpets. The Odina Mosque, built in the 16th century on the site of an older Mongol palace that had also been a prison, houses the regional museum. Kok Gumbaz, the Blue Dome, is the city's Friday mosque and resembles other Timurid mosques, including those of Shahrisabz. An old brick bridge crosses the Qashqadaryo River, and three madrassahs on one square were built between 1904 and 1915.
qatif: Qatif is a green oasis with rich agricultural soil, surrounded by palm groves and fed by many springs. The Persian Gulf lies to the east, with warm, calm waters rich in fish, shrimp and pearl oysters, and the ad-Dahna Desert to the west. The historic oasis shows archaeological evidence of settlement from about 3500 BCE. The name Qatif is derived from a word meaning 'harvest' or 'grain', and an older name, Al-Khatt, appears in the poetry of Antarah ibn Shaddad and Tarafa ibn Al-'Abd. Khatty became a preferred poetic word for 'spear', supposedly because the region was known for making them.

Qatif functioned for centuries as the most important trade port of Eastern Arabia, so that the whole Persian Gulf was called the 'Sea of Qatif'. It belonged to the Province of Bahrain with al-Hasa and the Bahrain islands. In 899 the Qarmatians conquered Qatif and al-Hasa and ruled until 1071. The Buyids raided Qatif in 988, and in 1059 it was freed from Qarmatian rule in the Battle of Qatif. The Uyunids held the region from 1071 until 1253, when the Usfurids took over. Ibn Battuta visited in 1331 and found a large, prosperous city. Power passed to the Jabrids of al-Hasa in 1440.

In 1520 the Portuguese sacked Qatif and killed the Jabrid ruler Muqrin ibn Zamil. The Ottomans took over in 1549, and the Portuguese conquered Qatif in 1551. The Banu Khalid ruled the region until 1790, when the First Saudi State took it, and the Second Saudi State held all of it from 1830. The Ottomans returned in 1871 and remained until 1913, when Ibn Saud established Saudi rule in the Eastern Province. Qatif Municipality was founded in 1926. In the 1920s the economy declined, first through the invention of cultured pearls, which hurt the Gulf pearl trade, and then through heavy taxes. After oil fields were developed in the late 1940s Qatif lost its status as an important port to Dammam.

Qatif is a governorate of the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia, covering about 481 square kilometres, with Qatif City as its seat. With al-Hasa it forms the historical core of the province, and it is the centre of the Shia population of Saudi Arabia. Most people are Arab Baharna, with a bedouin minority and some Sunni Gulf Arabs. The oasis keeps old villages such as Al-Awamia and Al-Qala'a and Tarout Castle, and the Ashura season and the children's custom of Qarqi'an are marked each year.
qena: Qena stands on the east bank of the Nile, about 95 km from El Balyana and 63 km north of Luxor. It lies close to the ruins of Dendera, the site of the Greco-Roman temples for which the region is best known. Luxor, a little to the south, is a long-established destination for visitors because of its temples and tombs and its position on the site of the ancient capital of Thebes. The climate is hot desert, with very hot summers and very little rain in any season. Winter days are warm and the nights cool, and the difference between day and night temperatures here is among the widest of any Egyptian city.

In antiquity the city was known in Greek as Kaine, meaning new city, which appears in Latin as Caene, and later as Maximianopolis. Gauthier identifies it with the ancient Egyptian town of Shabt. It is also linked with the name Caenepolis. Beside this Ancient Egyptian heritage Qena has a considerable Islamic one, with a number of mosques of distinctive architecture.

Its modern prosperity rests on the opening of the Wadi Qena towards the Red Sea, a major route between Upper Egypt and the coast. A road from the city crosses the Eastern Desert to the port of Safaga, and travellers between Luxor and the Red Sea pass through it, since there is only one good road connection. Qena is also noted for its pottery and is a large market town on the river.

Qena is the capital of the Qena Governorate. South Valley University has a campus in the city. It has one of the highest concentrations of Coptic Christians in Egypt, roughly 35 per cent of its population.
qianlong-emperor: Hongli, the future Qianlong Emperor, was the fourth son of the Yongzheng Emperor and was born to Noble Consort Xi. He was a favourite of both his grandfather, the Kangxi Emperor, and his father, and some historians argue that the Kangxi Emperor chose Yongzheng as his successor largely because Hongli was his favourite grandson. As a prince he was entrusted with important ritual tasks and included in court discussions of military strategy.

To prevent a succession struggle, the Yongzheng Emperor sealed the name of his chosen heir in a box behind the tablet over the throne in the Palace of Heavenly Purity. When he died suddenly in 1735, the will was read before the whole court and Hongli became emperor, taking the era name Qianlong, meaning Lasting Eminence.

Qianlong greatly expanded Qing territory through the Ten Great Campaigns, so that the empire grew to twice the size of the preceding Ming state. The Dzungar Khanate was defeated and the Tarim basin oasis states conquered; the two regions were joined and renamed Xinjiang. He ordered what is called the Dzungar genocide, and some scholars consider Qing expansion colonial in nature. Campaigns also reached Burma, Nepal and Vietnam, and rebellions in Jinchuan and Taiwan were suppressed.

He worked to preserve Manchu heritage, commissioning Manchu genealogies and dictionaries, and was a personal adherent of Tibetan Buddhism. He sponsored the Siku Quanshu, the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, but its compilation went with a literary inquisition: during about ten years some 3,100 works were burnt or banned, and the period saw 53 cases of literary persecution whose victims were executed or, if already dead, mutilated. In 1757 he made Guangzhou the only Chinese port open to foreign traders, beginning the Canton System.

In October 1795 Qianlong announced that he would abdicate the following spring, in order not to reign longer than his grandfather, who had ruled for 61 years. He passed the throne to the Jiaqing Emperor in 1796 but, as Emperor Emeritus, kept ultimate power until his death on 7 February 1799.

His reign came at the end of the High Qing era, the height of the dynasty's power and prosperity. At the same time, military weakness after constant warfare, endemic corruption and inefficiency at court brought the gradual decline of the empire.
qin-dynasty: The dynasty took its name from the state of Qin, a fief of the Zhou dynasty. According to the Shiji, Feizi was granted rule over the settlement of Qin in the 9th century BCE. In 770 BCE Duke Xiang escorted the Zhou court under King Ping in its emergency evacuation from Fenghao, and as a reward he led an expedition against the Western Rong and formally established Qin as a major vassal state, extending it eastward. Qin was a minor power for several centuries. Its strength grew greatly in the 4th century BCE, largely through the administrative and military reforms of Shang Yang, who sought a strong centralised state and a large army supported by a stable economy.

Beginning in 230 BCE King Ying Zheng conquered the rival states of the Warring States period, which culminated in unification in 221 BCE. He declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China. His government was highly bureaucratic. The empire was divided into 36 commanderies, aristocratic rule was ended, a Censorate was introduced to check officials, and a system of twenty ranks rewarded service in battle. Currency, weights, measures and writing were standardised, and the banliang coin became the first standardised currency used throughout China.

The state used the labour of hundreds of thousands of peasants and convicts to join the northern walls into what later became the Great Wall, to build a national road system, and to construct the Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang with its Terracotta Army. Three attempts were made on the emperor's life. He died in 210 BCE on a journey to the eastern frontiers while seeking an elixir of immortality.

The chief eunuch Zhao Gao and the prime minister Li Si hid the news, forged an order for the heir Fusu to commit suicide, and placed the younger son Huhai on the throne as Qin Er Shi. He executed many ministers, raised taxes and continued the great building projects. Popular revolt followed, and the weakened empire fell to the Chu generals Xiang Yu and Liu Bang, the latter of whom founded the Han dynasty.

The Qin existed for only 14 years, the shortest of any major dynasty, and had only two emperors. But the Han largely continued its military and administrative practices, and the Qin are credited as the originators of the Chinese imperial system that endured in some form until the Xinhai Revolution of 1911.
qin-shi-huang: Qin Shi Huang was born in Handan, the capital of Zhao, in 259 BCE as Ying Zheng or Zhao Zheng. According to the Shiji of Sima Qian, he was the eldest son of the Qin prince Yiren, a hostage at the court of Zhao who later became King Zhuangxiang of Qin. The Shiji also claims that he was the actual son of the merchant Lü Buwei. Modern scholars, among them Derk Bodde, doubt this and think the story was added to slander him.

King Zhuangxiang died in 246 BCE and was succeeded by his 13-year-old son. Lü Buwei acted as regent until 235 BCE, when Zhao Zheng assumed full power after Lü was banished for his involvement in a scandal with Queen Dowager Zhao. Lao Ai's attempted coup of 238 BCE failed, and Li Si became the new chancellor.

By 221 BCE he had conquered all the other warring states and unified China, and he took the new title huángdì rather than reuse the existing title for king. With Li Si he organised the empire into 36 commanderies, later 40, then counties, townships and hundred-family units, with appointments based on merit instead of hereditary right. They standardised weights and measures, the length of wagon axles and the currency, which became the Ban Liang coin, and the seal script of Qin became the standard for a universal written language. His public works included a national road system and the incorporation of the walls of several states into a single Great Wall.

He eliminated the Hundred Schools of Thought, and Legalism became the mandatory ideology. He is traditionally said to have banned and burned many books and executed scholars, and he fell ill and died during his fifth tour of eastern China.

The emperor died in July or August of 210 BCE at Shaqiu, aged 49. He had never written a will. Li Si and the eunuch Zhao Gao concealed his death, then forged a letter commanding his eldest son Fusu to commit suicide, and his younger son Hu Hai became the Second Emperor. His mausoleum, begun in 215 BCE, is guarded by the Terracotta Army.

Traditional Chinese historiography portrayed him as a brutal tyrant. Since the mid-20th century scholars have questioned this view, which stems partly from the harsh assessments of the Han dynasty that followed the Qin.
qing-empire: The Qing were founded not by Han Chinese, who made up the majority of the population, but by Manchus, a sedentary farming people descended from the Jurchens of the region now covering Jilin and Heilongjiang. Nurhaci, leader of the Jianzhou Jurchens and a vassal of the Ming, unified the Jurchen clans and founded the Later Jin dynasty in 1616, renouncing Ming overlordship. He established the Eight Banners military system. His son Hong Taiji, who renamed the Jurchens Manchus, was declared Emperor of the Great Qing in 1636.

Peasant rebels captured Beijing, but the Ming general Wu Sangui opened the Shanhai Pass to the Qing army, which defeated the rebels and took over the government in 1644 under the Shunzhi Emperor. Ming rump regimes and the Revolt of the Three Feudatories delayed complete conquest until 1683. The 61-year reign of the Kangxi Emperor, the longest of any emperor in Chinese history, began the High Qing era, and the reigns of the Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors marked the height of Qing power. At its height the empire stretched from the Sea of Japan to the Pamir Mountains.

After Qianlong's death the dynasty faced internal revolts, corruption and foreign intrusion. Defeat in the Opium Wars led the United Kingdom, France, Russia and the United States to force unequal treaties granting trading privileges, extraterritoriality and treaty ports. The Taiping Rebellion and the Dungan Revolt caused the deaths of over 20 million people. Defeat by Japan in 1895 cost the dynasty suzerainty over Korea and Taiwan, and the Late Qing reforms included the abolition of the imperial examination system in 1905. The Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 led to the Xinhai Revolution, and the Xuantong Emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912.

The dynasty was established by conquest and maintained by armed force. The Eight Banners gained Mongol and Han-martial banners, and the Ming troops that surrendered after 1644 formed the Green Standard Army, which eventually outnumbered the Banners three to one. The Lifan Yuan handled relations with Mongols and Tibetans, and the Canton System of 1756 restricted maritime trade to Guangzhou. The population, roughly 150 million in 1700, doubled over the next century, helped by New World crops such as maize and sweet potatoes.
qinghai-lake: Qinghai Lake lies about 100 kilometres west of Xining, in a hollow of the Tibetan Plateau at 3,205 metres above sea level, in north-eastern Qinghai. It is an alkaline endorheic salt lake: twenty-three rivers and streams run into it, most of them seasonal, but inflow is low and evaporation high, so its salt concentration is about 1.4 per cent by weight, against about 3.5 per cent in seawater. It became isolated from the Yellow River about 150,000 years ago.

The Chinese name 青海 combines a classical colour word covering both blue and green with the word for sea, a literal calque of the Mongolian Koko Nor, which did not distinguish lakes from larger bodies of water. The Tibetan name, Tso ngönpo, means Blue Lake or Sea.

Under the Han dynasty substantial numbers of Han Chinese lived in the Xining valley to the east. After its wars with the Xiongnu, Han China connected the lake for a time with the Western Sea of tradition, assumed to balance the East China Sea. In the 17th century the Mongolic-speaking Oirat and Khalkha migrated to Qinghai and became known as Qinghai Mongols, and in the 1620s Gushri Khan and other Khoshut Mongols moved to the area.

In 1724 the Qinghai Mongols under Lobzang Danjin revolted against the Qing dynasty. The Yongzheng Emperor put down the rebellion, ended Qinghai's autonomy, imposed direct rule and sent Manchu and Han settlers to dilute the Mongols. Under Nationalist rule, from 1928 to 1949, the Han formed a majority of the province's people, although Chinese Muslims dominated its government. The general Ma Bufang and the governor joined in a ceremony to worship the God of the Lake.

Qinghai Lake is the largest lake in China and gave its name to Qinghai Province. It lies on several bird migration routes across Asia, and the Bird Islands on its western side have been sanctuaries of the Qinghai Lake Natural Protection Zone since 1997. An island in the west holds a temple and hermitages, historically a Buddhist monastery, which monks and pilgrims reached only when the lake froze in winter. Pilgrims, mainly Tibetan Buddhists, still walk or ride around the lake, especially in every Horse Year of the twelve-year cycle.
qizilbash: The name comes from Turkish and means red head, after a crimson cap of twelve gores which marked adherence to the Twelve Imams and to Shaykh Haydar, head of the Safavid order. It began as a pejorative used by their Sunni Ottoman enemies and was taken up as a mark of pride. In the 15th century Haydar organised his followers into militant troops. They were at first drawn from seven Turkish-speaking tribes: the Rumlu, Shamlu, Ustajlu, Afshar, Qajar, Tekelu and Zulkadar. Their beliefs were heterodox: they regarded their Safavid leader as a manifestation of the divine, and orthodox Twelver Shia classed them as ghulat, extremists.

By the summer of 1500 about 7,000 supporters had rallied to the young Ismail at Erzincan. They overcame a force of 30,000 Aq Qoyunlu and took Tabriz. In 1510 the Qizilbash defeated the Uzbeks at Marv, but in 1512 an army was destroyed at the Battle of Ghazdewan after Turcoman Qizilbash mutinied against their Persian commander, Najm-e Thani. On 20 August 1514 the Ottoman sultan Selim I, whose army had firearms and cannon and was reported to outnumber them as much as three to one, defeated them badly at Chaldiran. The defeat destroyed Ismail's belief in his own invincibility and changed his relation to his followers.

For almost ten years afterwards rival Qizilbash factions fought for control of the kingdom, and the ten-year-old Tahmasp I, who succeeded in 1524, was at first the ward of the Qizilbash amir Ali Beg Rumlu. Tahmasp reasserted his authority, and the Qizilbash defended the kingdom against Uzbeks and Ottomans until the Peace of Amasya in 1555. Abbas I, who came to power in 1588, built a standing army and administration from Circassian, Georgian and Armenian ghulams and ended the independent rule of Turcoman chiefs in the provinces. By the end of his reign a fifth of the high-ranking amirs were ghulams.

The Qizilbash remained part of the Safavid army and administration, and the Afshar and Qajar rulers who followed the Safavids came from a Qizilbash background. By the 18th century the name was applied broadly to anyone in the service of the Safavid state. Many Qizilbash were settled in Kabul and Kandahar during the conquests of Nader Shah, and others joined the Mughal court. In Afghanistan the Qizilbash live mainly in cities such as Kabul, Kandahar and Herat; estimates of their number range from 30,000 to 200,000.
qu-yuan: The surviving evidence for Qu Yuan's life is limited. The earliest known reference is Jia Yi's Lament for Qu Yuan, written in 174 BCE. The first systematic biography is in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, which contains contradictory details and was probably influenced by Sima's own identification with Qu. According to Sima, Qu was a member of the Chu royal clan and served King Huai of Chu, who reigned from 328 to 299 BCE, as Left Minister.

King Huai exiled Qu Yuan to the region north of the Han River. He was later reinstated and sent on a mission to the State of Qi, to restore relations that the king had broken on the false pretext of King Hui of Qin, who had promised to cede territory near Shangyu. Under King Qingxiang, Prime Minister Zilan slandered him again, and he was exiled to the regions south of the Yangtze. In exile he is said to have collected legends and rearranged folk odes while writing some of the finest poetry in Chinese literature.

In 278 BCE he learned that General Bai Qi of Qin had captured the Chu capital, Ying, and is said to have written a long lament for it. He then died by suicide, wading into the Miluo River in Hunan while holding a rock. Chinese scholars debated his reason for centuries: the Song philosopher Zhu Xi suggested martyrdom for a falling homeland, others despair at the political situation in Chu.

Qu Yuan is the central figure of the Chu Ci anthology. The Li Sao, the Lament, is generally accepted as his work, while the attribution of many other poems has been disputed. The anthology was compiled and annotated by Wang Yi, who died in 158 CE, so the role Qu played in writing or editing the poems remains unclear. Chu stood on the southern fringe of the Chinese cultural area, and its poems keep traces of local traditions such as shamanism.

He is regarded as the first author of verse in China to have his name attached to his work, and as the originator of the sao style, which abandoned the four-character lines of the Shi Jing for lines of varying length. In the Han dynasty he became a model of the scholar-official denied the recognition his worth deserved. Popular legend says villagers beat drums and threw rice into the river to keep fish from his body, the origin given for zongzi and dragon boat racing on the fifth day of the fifth month.
quakers: Members of the Religious Society of Friends call one another Friends, after John 15:14. The name Quakers was first used by others, because George Fox told a judge to quake before the authority of God and because critics said that they shook or trembled while preaching. The movement arose in mid-17th-century England among dissenting Protestant groups that broke with the Church of England, many of which emerged during and after the English Civil War. In 1647 Fox claimed to have received a revelation that there is one, Christ Jesus, who can speak to a person's condition. He became convinced that a direct experience of Christ was possible without ordained clergy, and travelled through England, the Netherlands and Barbados preaching it.

The early preachers, above all the group known as the Valiant Sixty, travelled in Britain and overseas, and some were women. Quaker women published at least 220 texts in the 17th century, and Margaret Fell helped to define the movement. Persecution reached North America in July 1656, when Mary Fisher and Ann Austin began preaching in Boston; they were imprisoned for five weeks and banished by the Massachusetts Bay Colony. By 1700 the boisterous behaviour of the first years was no longer supported, and in the 18th century Quakers turned inward and converted fewer people.

Quakers were granted exemption from military service in Great Britain in 1757. In the early 1700s disquiet about slavery arose among Friends, many of whom in colonial America owned slaves, and the testimonies of Benjamin Lay, Anthony Benezet and John Woolman led to an abolition movement. Splits followed in America during the Revolutionary War and in the 19th century, and British Friends began missions in India in 1866.

Friends reject priests, hold to the priesthood of all believers and mostly believe in continuing revelation. Traditionally they wore plain dress, avoided alcohol, refused to swear oaths or take part in war, and used a plain calendar of numbered days and months. In unprogrammed worship there is no plan: Friends gather in expectant waiting, and anyone moved to speak stands and does so, with silence after each message. Others hold programmed worship with hymns, Bible readings and a pastor.

Decisions are taken at a meeting for worship for church business, in which members seek God's will. Quaker families founded the firms of Barclays, Lloyds, Clarks, Cadbury, Rowntree and Fry. In 1947 the British Friends Service Council and the American Friends Service Committee were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
quang-binh-province: Quảng Bình lies on the narrow coast of north-central Vietnam, with Hà Tĩnh to the north, Quảng Trị to the south, Laos to the west and the sea to the east. At its narrowest the province is only 40 kilometres from the sea to the Laotian border. Hills and mountains cover 85 per cent of it, and the Annamite Range forms the border with Laos, its highest peak, Phi Co Pi, rising to 2,017 metres. A belt of sand dunes along the coast acts as a natural dam against the tides. Most of its rivers rise in the Truong Son Range and flow to the sea, among them the Gianh and the Nhật Lệ.

Excavations show that people lived in the area in the Stone Age. In 1926 the French archaeologist Madeleine Colani excavated caves in the western mountains and assigned the finds to the Hòa Bình culture, with a radiocarbon date of 10,509 years ago, plus or minus 950. Some pottery from the Đông Sơn culture was also found. Under the Hùng kings the area belonged to the Việt Thường group.

King Chế Củ of Champa adopted a hostile policy toward the Vietnamese, and in 1068 he provoked a conflict. In February 1069 the fleet of King Lý Thánh Tông of Đại Việt scattered the Cham forces at the mouth of the Nhật Lệ River and took the Cham capital, Vijaya. Chế Củ was captured and secured his release only by ceding three districts, Bố Chính, Địa-ly and Ma-Linh, corresponding to present-day Quảng Bình and northern Quảng Trị. In 1469 the area became the Tân Bình prefecture, and in 1604 it was named Quảng Bình.

In the 17th century, during the Trịnh-Nguyễn war, the Gianh River became the border between Đàng Trong in the south and Đàng Ngoài in the north, and Đồng Hới was built as a fortress to protect the Nguyễn lords' territory. Quảng Bình became an important front. Under French rule it belonged to Annam. After the division of Vietnam in 1954 it was the southernmost province of North Vietnam, and during the Vietnam War it was the most heavily bombed province, by U.S. B-52s. In 1976 it was merged with Quảng Trị and Thừa Thiên into Bình Trị Thiên, and in 1990 the three were separated again.

On 12 June 2025 Quảng Bình was dissolved and merged with Quảng Trị province. Its capital was Đồng Hới. The Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng National Park, listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2003, protects a karst region with some 300 caves and grottoes, including the longest underground river, and Sơn Đoòng Cave is open only to limited guided tours.
quantum-mechanics: Quantum mechanics arose gradually from attempts to explain observations that classical physics could not account for. Scientific inquiry into the wave nature of light began in the 17th and 18th centuries, when Robert Hooke, Christiaan Huygens and Leonhard Euler proposed a wave theory of light, and in 1803 Thomas Young described the double-slit experiment, which played a major role in the general acceptance of that theory. Max Planck's solution to the black-body radiation problem and the correspondence between energy and frequency in Albert Einstein's paper on the photoelectric effect are the best-known early steps. These attempts, now called the old quantum theory, led in the mid-1920s to the full theory, developed by Niels Bohr, Erwin Schrödinger, Werner Heisenberg, Max Born, Paul Dirac and others.

The theory describes matter and light at and below the scale of atoms, where classical physics is insufficient. Quantum systems have bound states quantized to discrete values of energy, momentum and angular momentum, whereas classical systems can take them continuously. Measurements show characteristics of both particles and waves, and the uncertainty principle sets limits on how accurately the value of a physical quantity can be predicted before it is measured. In one formalism the wave function gives probability amplitudes for what measurements of a particle's energy, momentum and other properties may yield, and its change in time is described by the Schrödinger equation.

Several mathematically equivalent formulations exist. Dirac's transformation theory unifies the two earliest, Heisenberg's matrix mechanics and Schrödinger's wave mechanics, and Richard Feynman's path integral formulation treats an amplitude as a sum over all possible paths between an initial and a final state. Classical mechanics can be derived from quantum mechanics as an approximation valid at ordinary scales.

Quantum mechanics has been verified experimentally to an extremely high degree of accuracy. Quantum electrodynamics, the first complete quantum field theory, agrees with experiment to within 1 part in 10 to the power 12 for the magnetic properties of an electron. Solid-state physics and materials science depend on it, and its applications include quantum chemistry, superconducting magnets, light-emitting diodes, the optical amplifier, the laser, the transistor and the microprocessor, and imaging such as magnetic resonance imaging and electron microscopy.

Its counter-intuitive results have provoked philosophical debate since the start, centred on probability, wavefunction collapse and the measurement problem. The views of Bohr, Heisenberg and others are grouped as the Copenhagen interpretation, which treats the probabilistic nature of the theory as final rather than temporary. Steven Weinberg judged that there is no entirely satisfactory interpretation. Its formalism and that of general relativity contradict each other, and reconciling them has been a major goal of physics since the 20th century.
quanzhou: Quanzhou lies on a strip of land between the estuaries of the Jin River and the Luoyang River, where they flow into Quanzhou Bay on the Taiwan Strait. Foreign traders knew it as Zaiton or Zayton, from the Arabic name meaning City of Olives, which is traditionally linked to its Chinese epithet, the Coral-tree City, after the coral trees said to have been planted around it by its 10th-century ruler Liu Congxiao.

Quanzhou proper was established under the Tang in 718, and Muslim traders reached it early. After the fall of the Min state, the Qingyuan Circuit, with Quanzhou as its capital, was de facto independent from 949 to 978 under Liu Congxiao, who promoted overseas trade. In the first century of the Northern Song it became the starting point of the Maritime Silk Road, eclipsing Guangzhou. A 1095 inscription records two convoys of twenty ships each arriving from the Southern Seas every year, and celadon made for export accounted for ninety percent of Fujian's ceramic production. A report of 1206 lists merchants from Arabia, Iran, India, Sumatra, Java, Korea and Japan, and Tamil merchants built Hindu temples there.

Under the Yuan, a superintendent of foreign trade was established in 1277. Marco Polo recorded a 10 percent duty on the port's commerce and described it as one of the two chief havens for commerce in the world; Ibn Battuta ranked it first among the world's ports. Kublai Khan's invasions of Japan and Java sailed mainly from it. From 1357 a revolt by the Persian garrison against anti-Muslim laws lasted a decade and was followed by massacres of foreign communities. Under the Ming, foreign commerce was discouraged; piracy forced the Superintendency of Trade to close in 1522, and silting of the harbour later hindered larger ships.

Quanzhou is a prefecture-level city with a population of 8,782,285 at the 2020 census. In 2021 Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The Qingjing Mosque, which dates from 1009, is now a museum, and the Kaiyuan Temple has two five-storey pagodas of the 13th century. About 6 million overseas Chinese, most in Southeast Asia, trace their ancestry to the Quanzhou area.
quba: Quba is the administrative centre of the Quba District of Azerbaijan. It lies on the north-eastern slopes of the Shahdag mountain, at an altitude of 600 metres, on the right bank of the Kudyal River, 168 km from Baku. The city grew from a riverside village called Gudial. The Quba region has a humid subtropical climate. The great majority of its people are Azerbaijanis, with Tats and Lezgians as minorities.

European geographers and ancient Arabic and Albanian sources mention the place. A castle built by the ruler Anushiravan in the 11th century was called Bade-Firuz Qubat. Arabic sources of the 12th century name it Cuba, a geographical dictionary of the 13th century has Kubba, and sources of the 16th century call it Dome.

In the mid-18th century Hussain Ali moved his residence from Khudat and became khan of Quba, raising fortress walls around the city. He tried to create a state separate from the other Caucasian khanates. The Quba Khanate grew stronger under his son Fatali Khan, who reigned from 1758 to 1789. Like the other Transcaucasian khanates it was occupied by Czarist Russia in the early 19th century and formally annexed to the Russian Empire under the agreement of 1813. Quba was included in the Derbent province in 1840 and in 1860 became part of the Kuba Uyezd of the Baku Governorate. Alexandre Dumas, the orientalist Berezin, the writer Bestuzhev-Marlinsky and the Norwegian Thor Heyerdahl are said to have visited it.

Quba has long been a centre of carpet weaving: the carpet Golu Chichi was woven there in 1712 and has been shown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. In 2007 a mass grave was found of victims killed in 1918 during the events known as the March Days, and a memorial was opened on the site in 2013.

Quba's suburb of Qırmızı Qəsəbə, formerly Krasnaya Sloboda, meaning Red Town, is home to the largest community of Mountain Jews in Azerbaijan, one of the largest Jewish populations in the former Soviet Union. The city's red-brick Juma Mosque was erected in 1802, an octagonal building with a dome 16 m across. The Sakina-Khanum Mosque dates from 1854, and the Chuhur hamam is a bathhouse with a brick beehive dome, used until 1985. The bridge over the Kudyalchay, built in 1894 with 14 brick spans and a length of 275 m, is the only one of seven bridges once in the district to survive. Local cuisine reflects its multicultural history.
quedlinburg: Quedlinburg lies just north of the Harz mountains, mostly in the western part of the valley of the Bode, a river that flows from the Harz into the Saale. The town centre stands about 123 metres above sea level. Quedlinburg was the capital of its district until 2007, when the district was dissolved, and it has belonged to the state of Saxony-Anhalt since German reunification in 1990.

A settlement called Gross Orden stood on the eastern bank of the Bode by the early 9th century, and Quedlinburg was first mentioned as a town in 922, in a donation by King Henry the Fowler. According to legend, Franconian nobles offered Henry the German crown there in 919. After Henry's death in 936 his widow, Saint Matilda, founded a community of women on the castle hill, where daughters of the higher nobility were educated and whose main task was to pray for Henry and his successors.

In 973 an imperial assembly was held at the court, at which Mieszko, duke of the Polans, Boleslav, duke of Bohemia, and nobles from as far away as Byzantium and Bulgaria paid homage to Emperor Otto I. In 994 Otto III granted the town the rights of market, tax and coinage. Quedlinburg joined the Hanseatic League in 1426.

The abbey often disputed the town's independence, and in 1477 Abbess Hedwig expelled the forces of the Bishopric of Halberstadt, which had supported the town. The town then left the League and was protected by the Electorate of Saxony. Town and abbey became Lutheran in 1539. In 1697 Frederick Augustus I of Poland-Saxony sold his rights to the Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg for 240,000 thalers. After the abbey was secularised, Quedlinburg passed to Prussia. Its abbesses, who were free to marry, ruled the town until then; the last was the Swedish princess Sofia Albertina.

The old town, with about 2,000 half-timbered houses, is among the largest in Germany. The oldest, a timber-framed Ständerbau, dates from 1347. The castle hill, the collegiate church of St Servatius, a prime example of German Romanesque style, and the old town have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994. The church's treasure, stolen by an American soldier, was returned to Quedlinburg in 1993. The poet Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock was born in the town, which has more than 24,000 inhabitants.
queen-of-sheba: The Queen of Sheba, named Bilqis in Arabic and Makeda in Geʽez, is first mentioned in the Hebrew Bible, where her name is not given. She came to Jerusalem with a very great retinue, with camels bearing spices, very much gold and precious stones. Her story has been greatly elaborated in Judaism, Ethiopian Christianity and Islam. Modern historians and archaeologists place Sheba among the South Arabian kingdoms in what is now Yemen. Because no trace of her has been found, her existence is disputed.

Sources differ on where she came from. Josephus made her queen of Egypt and Ethiopia, and the Talmud says that the phrase malkath Sheba means the kingdom of Sheba, not a woman. The New Testament mentions a queen of the South who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, and in the Quran a speaker reports finding a woman ruling a people who bow to the sun instead of God.

Scholars date the biblical story variously. Many place its present form in the revision made during the Babylonian Captivity, about 550 BCE, and think its purpose was to glorify Solomon, although the Deuteronomic history is otherwise critical of him. The visit could conceivably have been a trade mission, since Solomon sought to settle on the Red Sea shore and so weaken the monopoly of Saba and other South Arabian kingdoms on the caravan trade, and Assyrian sources show that South Arabia traded internationally as early as 890 BCE.

The chronology is debated: Solomon lived from about 965 to 926 BCE, and some argue that the first traces of the Sabean monarchy come about 150 years later, though Peter Stein holds that the kingdom had emerged by the 10th century BCE.

South Arabian inscriptions mention a queen, but none names the Queen of Sheba, and excavations of the Sabaean temples of Awwām, known in folklore as the Sanctuary of Bilqis, found nothing connected with her. She became a popular subject of art. Twelfth-century cathedrals at Strasbourg, Chartres, Rochester and Canterbury show her, and in the Renaissance she appears on Ghiberti's doors of the Florence Baptistery and in Piero della Francesca's frescoes at Arezzo.
queen-victoria: Victoria was born on 24 May 1819, the daughter of Prince Edward, Duke of Kent and Strathearn, the fourth son of King George III. The death of Princess Charlotte of Wales in 1817 had caused a succession crisis that pressed the unmarried royal brothers to marry and have children. Victoria's father died in 1820, the year of her grandfather's death, and she was raised under close supervision by her mother and her mother's comptroller, John Conroy. She became heir presumptive when George IV died in 1830 and William IV succeeded him.

Victoria turned 18 on 24 May 1837, and William IV died on 20 June 1837, when she became queen. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days was longer than any of her predecessors' and gave its name to the Victorian era. On 10 February 1840 she married her maternal first cousin, Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, having proposed to him herself on 15 October 1839. Their nine children married into royal and noble families across Europe, which earned her the name grandmother of Europe.

After Albert's death in 1861 she went into deep mourning and avoided public appearances. British republicanism briefly gained strength during her seclusion, but her popularity recovered in the latter half of her reign.

After the Indian Rebellion of 1857 the East India Company was dissolved, and Victoria condemned atrocities on both sides. The Royal Titles Act 1876 gave her the title Empress of India from 1 May 1876, proclaimed at the Delhi Durbar on 1 January 1877. Her Golden Jubilee in 1887 marked fifty years since her accession, and her Diamond Jubilee was also a time of public celebration.

Victoria died at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight on 22 January 1901, aged 81, and was succeeded by her son Edward VII; she was the last British monarch of the House of Hanover. From 1832 she kept a detailed journal that eventually ran to 122 volumes; after her death her youngest daughter Beatrice edited the diaries and burned the originals, though much of the text survives in copies. Of her grandchildren, 34 survived to adulthood. Her youngest son Leopold had haemophilia B, and her daughters Alice and Beatrice were carriers, so the disease passed to several royal houses of Europe. Her great-grandsons included Alexei Nikolaevich, Tsarevich of Russia, and Alfonso, Prince of Asturias.
quelimane: Quelimane is a seaport and the administrative capital of Zambezia Province in Mozambique, as well as the province's largest city. It stands 25 km from the mouth of the Rio dos Bons Sinais, the River of the Good Signs, which Vasco da Gama is said to have named when, on his way to India, he reached it and saw good signs that he was on the right path. The town and much of the province are extremely prone to floods in the rainy season.

The town began as a Swahili trade centre and then grew as a slave market of the Indian Ocean slave trade. It was founded by Muslim traders, with a link to the Kilwa Sultanate, and was one of the oldest towns in the region. The origin of its name is obscure. One tradition says that in 1498 Vasco da Gama asked some labourers for the name of the place and they answered kuliamani, meaning we are cultivating. Another says the Portuguese named the settlement after an Arab, or half-Arab, interpreter, since kalimani in the Arabic of the East African coast means interpreter.

In 1761 the settlement became a town. Until 1853 trade was forbidden to anyone but the Portuguese. In the early 20th century Swiss planters organised sisal plantations, and the town grew, attracting Muslim and Indian communities and new infrastructure built by the Portuguese authorities. Its port exported mainly tea from the district of Zambezia, and coconut was also processed there. By 1970 Quelimane had 71,786 inhabitants. The town was the end point of David Livingstone's west-to-east crossing of south-central Africa in 1856, and Mozambique became independent from Portugal in 1975.

Portuguese is the official language of Mozambique, and the most common local language around Quelimane is Chuabo. The town has a large hospital, two cathedrals, a mosque and a public university for teachers. It is the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese, and other Christian churches and mosques are also present.
quetzalcoatl: The name comes from Nahuatl and means Precious serpent or Quetzal-feathered Serpent. The earliest known depiction of a feathered serpent is on Stela 19 at the Olmec site of La Venta, dated to around 900 BCE, where a serpent rises behind a person who is probably engaged in a shamanic ritual. It is probably not the same deity as the later one, but it shows that feathered snakes were a symbol in Mesoamerica from the Formative period on.

Teotihuacan was the first culture to use the feathered serpent as an important religious and political symbol, notably at the Quetzalcoatl temple in the Ciudadela complex. The earliest images show a real snake; among the Classic Maya the figure began to take human features, such as a beard. After the fall of Teotihuacan, around 600 CE, the cult spread to Xochicalco, Cacaxtla and Cholula, and images then appear at Chichén Itzá and El Tajín. Cholula remained the chief centre of his worship in the Postclassic period.

Among the Aztecs Quetzalcoatl was a creator deity linked to wind, the planet Venus, the Sun, merchants, crafts and learning, and the patron of the priesthood. The two chief priests of the Templo Mayor bore the title Quetzalcoatl Tlamacazqui. As Ehecatl he is the wind; as the morning star he is called Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli, and his twin Xolotl is the evening star.

He descended to Mictlan, the underworld, and made the people of the fifth world from the bones of earlier races, using blood drawn from his own body. He is credited with inventing books and the calendar and with giving maize to humankind. In the Codex Chimalpopoca, Tezcatlipoca makes him drunk on pulque; ashamed, he burns himself in a stone chest, and his heart rises as the morning star.

Since the sixteenth century it has been widely held that Moctezuma II took Hernán Cortés, landing in 1519, for the returning Quetzalcoatl. Many scholars, among them Matthew Restall and James Lockhart, regard this as one of the myths of the Spanish conquest. They note that it appears only in documents of Spanish influence, such as the Florentine Codex, written some fifty years after the conquest. Franciscans such as Toribio de Benavente equated the god with Thomas the Apostle.

Between 1200 and 1600 a confederacy of Eastern Nahuas, Mixtecs and Zapotecs kept a pilgrimage and commercial centre at Cholula, which the Spaniards compared to Rome and Mecca. It fought the Aztec Empire for nearly seventy-five years and supplied the Spaniards with an army.
quetzaltenango: Quetzaltenango is the capital of the department of the same name in western Guatemala. It stands at an elevation of 2,330 metres in a high-altitude volcanic basin of the Sierra Madre, encircled by the volcanic complexes of Santa María, Santiaguito and Cerro Quemado. It is part of the Los Altos Metropolitan Area, which includes Salcajá, Cantel, Almolonga, Zunil and other municipalities.

The name is Nahuatl and means the walled place of the quetzal bird; it became the city's official name in colonial times. Many of its people, especially the indigenous population, use the Kʼicheʼ name Xelajú, or Xela, from xe laju' noj, meaning under ten mountains. Some consider it, unofficially, the capital of the Mayas.

Before the Spanish conquest Quetzaltenango was a city of the Mam Maya, though by 1524 it had become part of the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom of Qʼumarkaj. It was said to have been over 300 years old when the Spanish arrived. With the help of his allies, the conquistador Pedro de Alvarado defeated and killed the Maya ruler Tecún Umán there.

From 1838 to 1840 the city was the capital of the state of Los Altos, one of the states of the Federal Republic of Central America. As the union broke up, the army of Rafael Carrera conquered the city and made it part of Guatemala. In 1850 it had about 20,000 people, and wheat was its largest export, followed by cacao, sugar, wool and cotton. During the 19th century coffee was introduced as a major crop, the local economy prospered, and much Belle Époque architecture survives in the city.

On 24 October 1902 the Santa María volcano erupted, and rocks and ash fell on the city an hour later. In 1930 the only electric railway in Guatemala, the Ferrocarril de Los Altos, was inaugurated, built by AEG and Krupp and linking Quetzaltenango with San Felipe, Retalhuleu. Mudslides soon destroyed it and it was demolished in 1933. A railway museum now stands in the city centre.

Quetzaltenango is the main economic, educational and cultural centre of the south-western Guatemalan highlands. At the 2018 census it had 180,706 inhabitants, and 43 percent of its population was indigenous Guatemalan in 2014. It is home to several universities, among them the Centro Universitario de Occidente San Carlos de Guatemala, and to the football club Club Xelajú MC. In 2008 the Central American parliament, PARLACEN, announced that the city would be the capital of culture of Central America every 15 September.
qufu: Qufu is a county-level city in south-western Shandong, about 130 kilometres south of the provincial capital Jinan. Its name means crooked hill and refers to a mile-long hill that was part of the city when it was the capital of Lu. Together with Zoucheng, the birthplace of Mencius, it is known as Zoulu. Confucius is traditionally believed to have been born at nearby Mount Ni. The small historical centre is enclosed by a restored Ming-era city wall and moats.

In the Shang period the area was home to the people of Yan, counted among the Eastern Barbarians or Dongyi. After King Wu of Zhou founded the Zhou dynasty, his younger brother Dan, the Duke of Zhou, was granted the land and became Duke of Lu. He stayed at the royal court and entrusted the rule to his son Bo Qin. After the people of Yan joined a failed rebellion around 1042 BCE, their territory became part of Lu, which kept Qufu as its capital throughout the Spring and Autumn period. In 249 BCE Chu conquered Lu.

In 1012 the county was renamed Xianyuan and moved some 4 kilometres east. The Jin dynasty restored the name Qufu in 1142, but the city stayed on that site until 1522, when the Jiajing Emperor of the Ming had the present city wall built. In the Southern Song the head of the Confucius family, Duke Yansheng Kong Duanyou, fled south to Quzhou, while the Jin appointed his brother Kong Duancao as duke at Qufu. Two dukes existed until the Yuan period, when Kublai Khan invited the southern duke to return; he refused, and the northern branch kept the title. In November 1966, during the Cultural Revolution, about 200 staff members and students of Beijing Normal University destroyed more than 6,000 artefacts in the city.

The three best-known sites are the Temple of Confucius, the Cemetery of Confucius and the Kong Family Mansion, known together as San Kong and listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994. The temple was consecrated by the Duke of Lu within two years of the death of Confucius. Its Dacheng Hall and nine courtyards on a central axis resemble the Forbidden City, and the complex has 460 rooms. The cemetery holds the tombs of more than 100,000 descendants of Confucius over about 2,000 years. In 1982 the State Council designated the city a national historical and cultural city.
quimper: Quimper is the prefecture of the Finistère department of Brittany in north-western France. It stands at the meeting of the Steir, Odet and Jet rivers, 62 km north-west of Lorient, 181 km west of Rennes and 486 km west-south-west of Paris. Its name comes from the Breton kemper, meaning confluence, a reference to the three rivers; the word is cognate with Welsh cymer. The Latin names were Civitas Aquilonia and Corisopitum, and the Breton name is Kemper. The climate is oceanic, with an average annual rainfall of about 1,214 mm.

The site was first settled in Roman times, when France was known as Gaul. By 495 it had become a bishopric, and the cathedral is dedicated to Corentin, a bishop of the fifth century and the first of Quimper. The town later became the capital of the counts of Cornouailles, the region of Cornouaille, which has a distinctive Breton-Celtic character; the historical name resembles that of Cornwall in southern England. In the eleventh century Cornouaille was united with the Duchy of Brittany.

The War of the Breton Succession (1341–1364) brought considerable ruin to the town, and in 1364 the duchy passed to the House of Montfort. Quimper's best-known product is Quimper faience, a tin-glazed pottery made here since 1690 using the bold provincial designs of Jean-Baptiste Bousquet. The town was also known for copper and bronze work, galvanised ironware, hosiery, leather, paper and woollen goods. In 1959 the commune absorbed the former communes of Ergué-Armel, Kerfunteun and Penhars. The physician René Laennec, inventor of the stethoscope, and the explorer Yves-Joseph de Kerguelen-Trémarec, who found the Kerguelen archipelago, were born in Quimper.

The Cathedral of Saint-Corentin was built between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries and is the oldest Gothic structure in lower Brittany. Its twin towers are 76 m high, and the spires were added in the nineteenth century. The Romanesque Church of Locmaria dates from the eleventh century, and ruins of the fifteenth-century town walls stand near the Episcopal palace, which holds the Musée départemental Breton. The Musée des beaux-arts has paintings from the fourteenth to the twenty-first century, including works by Peter Paul Rubens and by painters of the Pont-Aven School.

Quimper keeps Breton traditions alive: its Diwan schools teach in Breton, and the Festival de Cornouaille is held in the last week of July. The railway station is the terminus of a high-speed TGV line from Paris, a journey of about 3 hours 40 minutes.
quintana-roo: Quintana Roo is Mexico's easternmost state, on the eastern part of the Yucatán Peninsula, with a coast on the Caribbean Sea to the east and the Gulf of Mexico to the north. It is bordered by Campeche to the west, Yucatán to the northwest and Belize to the south. Its capital is Chetumal, and it is divided into 11 municipalities. The state includes the city of Cancún, the islands of Cozumel and Isla Mujeres, the town of Bacalar and the Sian Ka'an biosphere reserve, and it has four generalised ecosystems: tropical forest, savanna, mangrove and coral reef. Its exposed position makes it frequently subject to severe hurricanes.

The area was long part of Yucatán and shared its history. From about 2000 BCE the Maya transformed it into an agricultural forest, managing selected trees, and archaeological evidence shows ancient home gardens, managed tree plots and cacao groves. Ancient human remains have been found in submerged caves and sinkholes near Tulum, including a woman who lived at least 9,900 years ago, found in the Chan Hol cave in 2016, one of the oldest human skeletons found on the American continent.

Spanish colonisation affected the region from the 16th century. With the Caste War of Yucatán, which began in the 1840s, all non-Indigenous peoples were driven from the region, and the independent Maya nation of Chan Santa Cruz, based on what is now the town of Felipe Carrillo Puerto, kept considerable independence for decades, with separate trade and treaty relationships with British Honduras, now Belize.

President Porfirio Díaz created the Territory of Quintana Roo by decree on 24 November 1902, naming it after Andrés Quintana Roo, an early patriot of the Mexican Republic. The Mexican Federal Army subdued most of the Maya population during the 1910s. In 1913 the area was declared part of Yucatán again, but in 1915 it became a separate territory once more, and on 8 October 1974 it was granted statehood.

In the last quarter of the 20th century tourism, above all the development of Cancún, drove rapid growth in the north of the state, while the south kept a traditional economy of forestry and wood extraction. Many migrants have come from Yucatán, Campeche, Tabasco and Veracruz. The state holds the Maya sites of Chacchoben, Cobá, Kohunlich, Muyil, Tulum, Xel-Há, San Gervasio and Xcaret.
quintus-curtius-rufus: Apart from his name on the manuscripts, nothing about Curtius Rufus is definitely known. His Histories is isolated in Roman literature, since no other ancient text is known to mention either the work or its author. Its date rests wholly on internal evidence. Book X praises the blessings of peace under Roman imperial rule, and its mention of the Parthian Empire, which lasted from 247 BCE to 224 CE, gives outer limits. A passage contrasting the succession crises of Alexander's generals with a Roman civil war averted by the quick appointment of an emperor has been read as the night of 24-25 January 41 CE, when Claudius was declared emperor. Many modern scholars accept the middle to late first century CE.

By his name he would have belonged to the Curtii Rufi, a branch of an old patrician family. One plausible candidate is a Curtius Rufus who was consul suffectus from October to December 43 CE under Claudius. Tacitus has him serving on the staff of a quaestor in Africa and as a protégé of Tiberius, and implies that he may have been of low birth.

His Historiae Alexandri Magni, the Histories of Alexander the Great, was written in ten books. Books I and II are entirely missing, with further gaps in Books V, VI and X. The work survives in 123 codices, all derived from one incomplete exemplar of the ninth century. It rarely names its sources, though it mentions Cleitarchus twice and Ptolemy and Timagenes once each; works built on such accounts are grouped as the Vulgate tradition of Alexander historiography. Peter Pratt has suggested that it was left unpublished because of its themes of conquest, rebellion and imperial ambition.

The work became popular in the High Middle Ages and was a principal source for the Alexander Romance, including Walter of Châtillon's epic poem Alexandreis. It was admired in the Italian Renaissance, and painters such as Paolo Veronese and Charles Le Brun drew on episodes from it. The first printed edition was made at Venice by Vindelinus Spirensis in 1470 or 1471, and Edmund Hedicke's edition of 1867 set a convention that remains influential.
quipu: The word quipu comes from a Quechua word meaning 'knot'; khipu is the spelling that reflects Quechua and Aymara. A claim that a proto-quipu exists at the Late Preceramic site of Caral, from about 3000-1800 BCE, has not been thoroughly evaluated. A more plausible precursor is the wrapped batons from Cerrillos of the Late Paracas period, about 350-200 BCE. The first undisputed quipus belong to the Middle Horizon, about 600-1000 CE, and are attributed to the Wari Empire. Wari specimens tend to be smaller and have brightly coloured thread wrapped around the cords, and they used a system of knots that scholars do not fully understand.

A quipu usually consists of cotton or camelid fibre cords and holds information sorted by dimensions such as colour, order and number. It can have anything from a few cords to several thousand. In the numerical system Leslie Leland Locke first showed, and Marcia Ascher and Robert Ascher later analysed on several hundred examples, knots are tied in clusters along the cord and the position of a cluster gives a power of ten.

Simple knots in a row stand for tens and higher digits, a long knot with extra turns for the digits 2 to 9 in the ones position, a figure-eight knot for 1, and the absence of a knot for zero. So 731 is written as 7s, 3s and E.

How non-numerical information was recorded is disputed. Gary Urton has suggested a binary system that could record phonological or logographic data, while Frank Salomon argues for a system of representative symbols. A 2005 report identified a sequence of three figure-eight knots at the start of a quipu that may name Puruchuco, its keeper or its subject.

Under the Inca Empire, specialists called quipucamayocs made and read quipus. They carried out addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, tracked the mita labour tax and economic output, ran the census and kept the calendar.
