Inca historians also used quipus when they told the Spanish about the past, though it is unknown whether the cords held the story itself or only key numbers.

After the Spanish conquest began in 1532, officials at first relied on quipus to settle disputes over tribute, and quipucamayocs could be summoned to court. The Third Council of Lima ordered some burned in 1583 as idolatrous because they recorded offerings to non-Christian gods. Some priests promoted their use, and quipu boards joined knots with writing. Just under 1,400 pre-Columbian quipus are known today, and some Andean villages still display them as communal heritage.
quirigua: Quiriguá is a medium-sized site of about 3 square kilometres, with its ceremonial centre about a kilometre from the north bank of the lower Motagua River. It lies 48 kilometres north of Copán. The river has since changed course and now flows a kilometre south of the centre, and the flood plain exposed the site to periodic flooding.

The local bedrock is a hard red sandstone that does not shear or fracture easily, which let sculptors erect the tallest freestanding stone monuments in the Americas. It stood where the trade route from the highlands to the Caribbean coast met the route from Copán to the Petén cities, and it could control the trade in uncut jade, cacao and obsidian along the river.

Late Preclassic artifacts show occupation before 200 CE, and the acropolis was begun by about 550. No monuments were raised from 495 to 653. In the 6th or early 7th century a flood buried the surface of the site in silt, and a smaller complex became the new centre. The first new monument in a century and a half was raised in 653 by the king K'awiil Yopaat.

In 724 Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil of Copán installed K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat on the throne of Quiriguá as his vassal. By 734 the king called himself k'ul ahaw, 'holy lord', and in 736 he received a visit from Wamaw K'awiil, the high king of Calakmul, which suggests that Calakmul backed his rebellion in order to weaken Tikal, an old ally of Copán. In 738 he captured the Copán king, who was sacrificed in the Great Plaza at Quiriguá. The city kept its independence, and its population and building grew rapidly, though the population never exceeded about 1,200 to 1,600 in the centre.

The city's power waned under its last recorded ruler, Jade Sky, whose two stelae are stunted. The last hieroglyphic texts date from 810, when Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat of Copán visited to carry out a k'atun-ending ritual. Quiriguá then lost its reason to exist as trade stopped flowing along the Motagua, and it was nearly deserted within a few years. People linked to the Yucatán coast briefly reoccupied it in the early Postclassic, about 900 to 1200, and added to the acropolis.

Quiriguá lies in the municipality of Los Amates, department of Izabal, in south-eastern Guatemala, a little over 200 kilometres north-east of Guatemala City. It has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1981.
quito: Quito lies in the northern highlands of Ecuador, in the Guayllabamba river basin, on a long plateau on the eastern flanks of Pichincha, an active stratovolcano. The valley is flanked by volcanoes, some of them snow-capped. Pichincha has several summits, among them Ruku Pichincha at 4,700 metres and Guagua Pichincha at 4,794 metres. The city is about 40 kilometres long and five kilometres wide at its widest, so its main avenues run from north to south. Because of its altitude and its position on the equator the climate is cool and fairly constant, with a dry season from June to August and a wet season from September to May.

The oldest traces of human presence near Quito were excavated in 1960 by the American archaeologist Robert E. Bell at El Inga, on the slopes of the Ilaló volcano. Hunter-gatherers left obsidian tools there that are dated to 8000 BCE. Settled populations are thought to have lived in the area between 4400 and 1600 BCE. In the late fifteenth century the Inca Emperor Huayna Capac defeated the Quitu, the region's original inhabitants, and made Quito the capital of the empire's northern region.

Inca resistance to the Spanish continued in 1534. Diego de Almagro founded Santiago de Quito on 15 August 1534 at Colta, near Riobamba, and renamed it San Francisco de Quito on 28 August. The city was refounded at its present site on 6 December 1534 by 204 settlers led by Sebastián de Benalcázar, who captured the leader Rumiñahui, effectively ending organized resistance. Rumiñahui was executed on 10 January 1535. The Spanish conquest of 1534 is the date most often cited as the city's official founding, which makes Quito the oldest capital in South America.

In the republican period Quito saw political violence. Members of the Society of Free Inhabitants of Quito were assassinated by the government in 1833 after conspiring against it, and the Marcist Revolution began on 6 March 1845. President Gabriel García Moreno was assassinated in the city in 1875, and Archbishop José Ignacio Checa y Barba was killed by poison while celebrating Mass in 1877.

Quito is the capital of Ecuador and of Pichincha province, and the country's major governmental, administrative and cultural institutions are within it. Its historic centre, on 320 hectares, is the largest, least altered and best preserved in the Americas, with about 130 monumental buildings of mostly religious art and sculpture. It was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO on 18 September 1978, together with Kraków as the first to be so named. The equator runs through the northern part of the metropolitan area.
quotations-from-chairman-mao-tse-tung: The book grew out of Lin Biao's practice of building the study of Mao Zedong's texts into the daily drills of the People's Liberation Army. In 1961 Lin required the PLA Daily to print a Mao quotation each day, using an index of Mao's quotes arranged by topic that the Tianjin Daily had made, and this index became the core of the book. In December 1963 a deputy editor-in-chief of the PLA Daily proposed a selection in book form, and the first draft was 200 Quotations from Chairman Mao.

In May 1964 the General Political Department issued an internal edition with 355 quotations under 30 topics, and endorsement leaves written by Lin Biao. The definitive 1965 version has 427 quotations in 33 thematic chapters, taken from Mao's speeches and writings of 1929 to 1964 and drawing heavily on about two dozen documents in the four volumes of his Selected Works. From August 1965 copies had red vinyl covers, and most editions were small enough for a pocket.

The first print run of 4.2 million copies went only to the army, and 12 million had been printed by August 1965. In August 1966 the People's Publishing House took over printing and sold the book through Xinhua Bookstores, and provinces were ordered to build hundreds of new printing houses. On National Day in 1966 one million copies were handed to Red Guards who had travelled to Beijing, and people often swore oaths on the book.

It was approved for export in 1966 and, by May 1967, bookstores in 117 countries and territories were distributing it, in more than 50 languages. From the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s it was the most printed book in the world, and sources put the total at billions of copies.

Emphasis on the book decreased after the 9th Party Congress in April 1969. On 12 February 1979 the Publicity Department of the Chinese Communist Party ordered publication stopped, stating that the book distorted Mao Zedong Thought and had a widespread and pernicious influence. Today it is mostly nostalgia in China and is hard to find in bookstores. Abroad it was taken up in the French Maoist context, by African American and Asian American radicals in the United States, who sold copies in Berkeley in 1967, and in India by Charu Majumdar in the Naxalite movement.
quran: Muslims believe the Quran was revealed orally by God to Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over some 23 years, ending in 632 CE, the year of his death. Islamic tradition relates that the first revelation came in 610 CE in the Cave of Hira, on the Laylat al-Qadr, during one of his retreats to the mountains. According to tradition, several of Muhammad's companions served as scribes. Shortly after his death the Quran was compiled on the order of the first caliph, Abu Bakr, by companions who had written down or memorised parts of it. The caliph Uthman, who reigned from 644 to 656, established a standard version, the Uthmanic codex, which is generally considered the archetype of the Quran known today.

Some scholars argue that manuscript evidence, textual variants such as the Sanaa manuscript, and historical sources suggest a more gradual and complex process of compilation. Some textual critics hold that there never was a single original text, and Sunni and Shia accounts of its origins differ. Canonical variant readings, the qirāʾāt, are transmitted orally and differ only slightly in wording.

The text has 114 chapters, called sūrahs, made up of verses, called āyahs. The most popular Hafs version has 6,236 verses. The chapters are not in chronological order but roughly in order of decreasing size, and each except the ninth begins with the Bismillah, 'In the name of God'. Traditional accounts classify chapters as Meccan or Medinan, depending on whether they were revealed before or after Muhammad's migration to Medina.

The content covers basic beliefs such as the existence of God and the resurrection, narratives of earlier prophets, ethical and legal subjects, events of Muhammad's time, charity and prayer. Its style is allusive: events are referred to but not narrated, and people and places are mentioned but rarely named. For this reason Muslims rely on tafsir, or commentary, to explain it, together with the hadiths, oral traditions believed to record the words and actions of Muhammad.

In prayer the Quran is recited only in Arabic, ideally with a special prosody called tajwid. A person who has memorised the whole text is called a hafiz. Before printing was widely adopted in the 19th century it was copied by hand. The earliest manuscripts were in Hijazi script, and Kufic scripts with thicker strokes probably appeared in the ninth century. From the 11th century naskh, muhaqqaq and rayḥānī styles dominated, with the Maghribī style popular in North Africa and Iberia. Because copies were costly, they were often kept in mosques, frequently as a series of 30 parts, and Ottoman copyists were highly productive. Translating the text has always been considered difficult, since an Arabic word may have a range of meanings depending on context.
quraysh: According to traditional Arab sources, the Quraysh descend from Fihr ibn Malik, of the Kinana tribe, whose line is traced back to Adnan the Ishmaelite, regarded in tradition as the father of the northern Arabs. The tribe gained its name when Qusayy ibn Kilab, a sixth-generation descendant of Fihr, gathered his kinsmen and took control of the Kaaba, then a major pagan sanctuary in Mecca. Medieval Muslim sources agree that he made the Quraysh the dominant power in Mecca and assigned quarters to the clans. At first the Meccan economy rested on pilgrimage to the Kaaba rather than trade, and a dispute over his succession split the tribe into two factions.

Toward the end of the 6th century the Quraysh and Kinana fought the Fijar War against Qaysi tribes, whose aim, according to W. Montgomery Watt, was control of the trade routes of Najd. By about 600 CE the Quraysh leaders were prosperous merchants with something like a monopoly of the trade between the Indian Ocean and East Africa on one side and the Mediterranean on the other. They sent caravans to Yemen in winter and to Gaza, Bosra and Damascus in summer. The clans of Makhzum and Umayya acquired the most wealth, and the Umayyads were the strongest.

Muhammad was born into the Banu Hashim. The Quraysh at first showed little concern at his preaching but opposed him as he challenged the polytheism of Mecca. After the Hijra to Medina they fought him at Badr, Uhud and the Trench. A ten-year truce, the Treaty of al-Hudaybiya, was broken when a group among the Quraysh, against the advice of their chief Abu Sufyan, supported a client clan against allies of Muhammad. Muhammad entered Mecca virtually unopposed in 630, and almost all its inhabitants adopted Islam.

Muhammad brought the Quraysh into the ruling elite of the Muslim community, and the historian Fred Donner suggests that their organisational skills improved his statecraft in his last years. After his death in 632 a hadith holding that the caliph must come from the Quraysh became almost universally accepted, except among the Kharijites, and control of the state became a struggle between Qurayshi factions: the Banu Umayya under Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the Banu Hashim under Ali, and others. The Umayyads won the Second Fitna in 692 or 693. In 750 the Abbasids, a branch of the Banu Hashim, defeated them and killed many of the Banu Umayya.
qusayr-amra: Qusayr 'Amra, also written Quseir Amra or Qasr Amra, is the best known of the desert castles of eastern Jordan. It stands on the north side of Highway 40, about 85 kilometres from Amman and 21 kilometres south-west of Al-Azraq. What survives is the remnant of a larger complex of about 25 hectares that included a castle meant as a royal retreat, without military function, of which only the foundation remains. Its placement was governed by access to the ancient routes running north from Arabia to Syria, including the one from Tayma through Wadi Sirhan to the plain of Balqa.

A painting of six kings that includes the Visigothic king Roderic, who reigned 710 to 712, led researchers for a long time to date the building to about 710 and to the caliph Walid I. An inscription found in 2012 dated it to the two decades from 723 to 743, when it was commissioned by Walid ibn Yazid, crown prince under the caliph Hisham and caliph himself in 743 and 744. Walid and Yazid, two princes who each later became caliph, spent long periods away from Damascus, the Umayyad capital, before taking the throne.

The surviving building is a small hall and bathhouse of limestone and basalt, made of rough masonry bound with gypsum-lime mortar in a Sasanian tradition. The bathhouse is one of the oldest surviving remains of a hammam in the historic Muslim world. Its frescoes, mostly on the ceilings, show hunting, bathing and dancing scenes, working craftsmen, animals and plants, and a cycle of Jonah, the earliest known images of Jonah in Islamic art. The six kings are identified as the Byzantine emperor, Roderic, the Sasanian shah, the Negus of Ethiopia and the emperor of China, and their meaning is unclear, though a Greek word for victory found nearby suggests the caliph's supremacy over his enemies.

The hemispherical dome of the hot room shows the zodiac and 35 identifiable constellations, believed to be the earliest image of the night sky painted on anything other than a flat surface. Its only discernible error, the counterclockwise order of the stars, suggests it was copied from a flat original.

Alois Musil rediscovered the abandoned building in 1898, and drawings of the frescoes by Alphons Leopold Mielich in his book made them known. A Spanish team restored the frescoes in the 1970s, and the shellac applied then was removed in 1996. UNESCO inscribed the site as a World Heritage Site in 1985. A conservation project begun in 2010 by the World Monuments Fund, an Italian institute and the Department of Antiquities of Jordan also covers the exterior buildings, and cleaning has revealed rich colours.
qutb-minar: The Ghurids, a clan from Ghur in what is now western Afghanistan, annexed Multan and Uch in 1175-76 and Sindh in 1185-86. In 1193 Qutb al-Din Aibak conquered Delhi. After the defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan, the last Hindu ruler of Delhi before the conquest, he began a victory tower to mark the start of Islamic rule in the region. It rose over the ruins of the Lal Kot, the citadel of Dhillika, after the neighbouring Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque. The Minaret of Jam in Afghanistan, of about 1190, is a decade or so older.

Aibak finished only the first storey. His successor and son-in-law Shamsuddin Iltutmish added three more. After lightning damaged the top, Firuz Shah Tughlaq replaced it, added another storey and a cupola. The name is usually taken from Aibak, though it may honour the Sufi saint Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki, to whom Iltutmish was devoted.

The tower is 72.5 metres high and tapers from a base 14.3 metres across to 2.7 metres at the top. Its fluted shaft has stalactite-like bracketing under the balconies, and bands of inscriptions in naskh script carry Quranic verses and the titles of the Ghurid rulers Ghiyath al-Din and Mu'izz al-Din. Hindu craftsmen worked under Muslim architects, and some inscriptions are disarranged Quranic passages, since the craftsmen did not know the text.

Beside it stands the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, begun by Aibak in 1199, the earliest surviving mosque built by the Delhi sultans. It was built with columns from 27 Jain and Hindu temples, as Aibak's own inscription records. In its courtyard stands an iron pillar with a Sanskrit inscription of the fourth century CE, set up as a standard of the god Vishnu.

An earthquake damaged the minaret in 1505 and Sikandar Lodi repaired it. In 1828 Major Robert Smith renovated it and added a cupola, which was taken down in 1848 and re-erected on the ground nearby as Smith's Folly. Scholars have called the tower the earliest and best example of a fusion of Hindu and Muslim traditions. The Qutb complex became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993. After a stampede on the dark staircase on 4 December 1981 killed 45 people, mostly schoolchildren, the tower was closed to the public.
qutb-ud-din-aibak: Aibak came from Turkestan and belonged to a Turkic tribe of the same name, a word derived from the Turkic terms for moon and lord. Separated from his family as a child, he was taken to the slave market of Nishapur, where a qazi, Fakhruddin Abdul Aziz Kufi, bought him. He was treated affectionately, educated with the qazi's sons and taught archery, horse-riding and Qur'an recital. He was resold to a merchant, who sold him to the Ghurid Sultan Muhammad Ghori at Ghazni. He rose to be Amir-i Akhur, officer of the royal stables, and after being captured by Khwarazmian scouts and held in an iron cage he was released and favoured by the Sultan.

Aibak served at the first and second battles of Tarain, and after the Ghurid victory of 1192 Muhammad Ghori placed him over the former Chahamana territory at Kuhram. He took Meerut, Baran and Delhi in 1192; in 1193 he deposed the Tomara ruler there and took direct control. He fought in the campaign against the Gahadavala king Jayachandra, defeated the Chaulukya army at Mount Abu in 1197 and plundered Anhilwara, and besieged Kalinjar in 1202. His campaigns involved the large-scale capture of slaves; Hasan Nizami gives 20,000 for Gujarat and 50,000 for Kalinjar, figures that Irfan Habib thinks exaggerated.

After Muhammad Ghori was assassinated in March 1206, the citizens of Lahore asked Aibak to take sovereign power, and he informally ascended the throne on 25 June 1206. He disputed Ghurid territory with his father-in-law Taj al-Din Yildiz and at one point took Ghazni. In 1208 to 1209 Ghiyasuddin Mahmud sent him a ceremonial parasol and a deed recognising him as ruler of Hindustan.

In 1210 Aibak fell from his horse while playing chaugan, a form of polo, at Lahore and died when the pommel of the saddle pierced his ribs. He left no named heir. Turkic officers appointed Aram Shah, who ruled no more than eight months before Iltutmish, Aibak's former slave and son-in-law, defeated him and made the loosely held territories into the Delhi Sultanate. The line is called the Mamluk or Slave dynasty, though only Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban were slaves.

Contemporary chroniclers praised his generosity, which earned him the epithet lakh-bakhsh. The Qutb Minar in Delhi was begun in his reign, and the Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra in Ajmer is also attributed to him. His tomb is in Anarkali Bazaar, Lahore.
